film: À bout de souffle (Godard, 1960) and The Conversation (Coppola, 1974)
tek_cumle: Editing and sound are two invisible hands that shape how the viewer constructs space, time and meaning; this week you learned to make those hands visible, and today we put that to the test.

bolumler.baslik: A short review of the week
bolumler.html: This week we covered two large areas: editing and sound. In editing, we looked at the four kinds of relations (graphic, rhythmic, spatial, temporal), the continuity system and its tools (the 180° rule, the eyeline match, shot/reverse shot). In sound, we examined whether a sound’s source lies in the story world or not (diegetic / nondiegetic), onscreen and offscreen sound, and the sound bridge that links two scenes. The films: Breathless (À bout de souffle, Godard, 1960) and The Conversation (Coppola, 1974). Do the quiz first, then move on to the short-answer questions, and write the analysis task last. The answer key is at the very end; don’t look at it until you’ve finished the quiz.

quiz.soru: What is the basic goal of classical continuity editing?
secenekler: To make cuts conspicuous and remind the viewer that the film has been edited
To make space and time consistent and easy to read, directing attention to the story and keeping the cut unnoticed
To shoot every scene in as few shots as possible
To create a deliberate clash between image and sound
quiz.aciklama: The continuity system makes space and time legible and keeps attention on the story by rendering the cut invisible.

quiz.soru: What does the 180° rule exist to preserve?
secenekler: That the actors look the same tone under the lighting
That shots are equal in length
Consistent onscreen positions and directions of movement for the characters, by staying on one side of the axis of action
That the camera always stays at eye level
quiz.aciklama: Staying on one side of the axis keeps the characters’ left/right positions and directions of movement constant.

quiz.soru: In one shot a character looks offscreen; the next shot shows a letter on a table. The viewer assumes the character sees the letter. What is this technique?
quiz.aciklama: The link created between a look and the object being looked at is the eyeline match.

quiz.soru: In a conversation between two people, the camera shows one of them, then, from the same side of the axis, the other, and keeps alternating like this. What is this pattern called?
quiz.aciklama: Alternating cuts between speakers form the shot/reverse-shot pattern; it usually works together with the 180° rule.

quiz.soru: Which is the most accurate definition of a jump cut?
secenekler: Alternating between actions in two different locations
Cutting the same subject with little or no change in camera position, producing a noticeable leap in time and in the image
A scene’s sound beginning before its image
Linking the shape of an object to a similar shape in the next shot
quiz.aciklama: A jump cut cuts the same subject with a very small change of angle, creating a leap in time and position.

quiz.soru: Cutting from a round object in one shot to another, similarly shaped object in the next shot is the best example of which kind of editing relation?
quiz.aciklama: A connection built on visual similarities such as shape, color or line is a graphic relation.

quiz.soru: In a suspenseful scene, orchestral music swells although there is no musician or radio in the scene. What type of sound is this?
quiz.aciklama: Music whose source is not in the story world is nondiegetic sound.

quiz.soru: The frame shows only a woman sitting in a room; from behind the door we hear footsteps and a man’s voice. How is this sound classified?
quiz.aciklama: Its source is in the story world but not in the image: offscreen diegetic sound.

quiz.soru: At the end of a scene, before the image changes, we begin to hear the train whistle from the next scene; then a cut takes us to the station. What is this?
quiz.aciklama: The next scene’s sound beginning early is a sound bridge; it links the two scenes smoothly.

quiz.soru: In terms of this week’s sound concepts, what does Harry Caul’s repeated listening to the same recording in The Conversation show most of all?
secenekler: That recorded sound is not objective evidence but material that is selected, processed and interpreted
That nondiegetic music always carries the character’s emotion
That sound is independent of editing and produces no meaning
That the 180° rule applies to sound as well
quiz.aciklama: The film shows the recording taking on different meanings as it is replayed; sound, too, is selected, processed and interpreted.

sorular: What is the purpose of continuity editing? (2–4 sentences; refer to at least two techniques by name.)
Which rule does the jump cut break, and what effect does it create? (Name the rule and describe the effect in terms of the viewer’s experience.)
Give an example of a sound bridge. (From any film you’ve seen; describe which scene the sound carries over from and into, and what purpose this serves.)
analiz:
Task: Compare a jump-cut scene from Breathless (À bout de souffle) with the rules of classical continuity.

How to write it (300–500 words):

  • Choose and describe the scene: Which scene is it, roughly where in the film, who is in it, and what happens? How many cuts did you notice?
  • Imagine the classical solution: If we shot the same scene using the Hollywood continuity system, what would we do? Describe it using at least two tools such as the establishing shot, shot/reverse shot, the 180° rule and the match on action.
  • Name the difference: Which rule does Godard break, and how? Is time skipping, is position jumping, and how does the sound relate to the image (does it carry on over the cuts)?
  • Interpret the effect: What does this rupture create in the viewer: unease, energy, awareness of the editing, the character’s state of mind? Is it a “mistake” or a deliberate style? Give your reasons.

Assessment criteria: using the concepts correctly, concrete observation (seconds, shots, details of sound), actually carrying out the comparison with the classical system, and grounding your interpretation in observation.

Write down your answers — we’ll go over them.

terimler.tanim: The classical editing system that keeps cuts unnoticed and presents space and time consistently.
The principle that the camera stays on one side of an imaginary line through the scene to preserve screen direction.
A cut from a character who is looking to a shot showing what they are looking at.
A leap in time and in the image created by cutting the same subject from nearly the same angle.
The distinction between sound whose source lies in the story world and sound coming from outside that world (e.g. the film score).
The sound of one scene carrying over into the next, or the next scene’s sound beginning early.

yarin: Week 5 begins: with the question “What is film theory?” we turn to Stam’s introduction and to the “prehistory” of film theory — moving from analyzing form to the theories that think about it.
